title: Side-Channel Attacks Revisited - an Optimization Problem Perspective: Bootstrapping and Space Reduction
authors: Erez Tamir, Osnat Keren, and Itamar Levi
abstract:
Side-channel analysis (SCA) attacks rely on leakage from a target device. It is common to assume that linear operations implemented by XOR gates produce symmetric leakage and carry negligible side-channel information. In practice, leakage from XOR gates produces complex, non-independent, and time-varying asymmetric behavior. 

The paper introduces Feature Estimation based Attacks (FEbA) -- a dedicated profiling attack that exploits these asymmetries. The attack is versatile; it was demonstrated to be successful against the sharing and refreshing phases in masking-based implementations by greatly narrowing the guessing key space, with no access to intermediate values.

Such attacks have implications for designs such as ASCON, GIBBON, and ACE, where XORs that utilize the key are vulnerable to attacks regardless of the inherent SCA protection levels used in them (e.g., sponge $rate$, the leak-free components for re-keying, and masking order $d$).  

Experimental results indicate that the entropy of a $32$-bit key can be reduced below $1$ bit using (up to) $20,000$ traces from a standalone XOR without any access to intermediate values, or below $500$ traces with access to intermediate values.

1    Introduction
A central challenge in side-channel analysis (SCA) research is to take a set of adversarial
capabilities and constraints and translate them into a practical methodology for extracting
information about some targeted binary secret (key). These capabilities may include access
to current leakages, knowledge of algorithm inputs, or visibility into specific machine-level
instructions sequence, and perhaps additional abilities such as injecting faults into the
hardware. SCA adversaries must process large amounts of information and evaluate many
keys to extrapolate a likely key candidate. As a consequence, the runtime of attacks
may quickly exceed the processing capabilities of modern processors, whether in terms
of runtime or storage. As such, adversaries must significantly divide and conquer and
take measures like key divisions, reduce data-complexity by dimensionality reduction or
pruning points of interest (POI), and more.
    Much effort has been invested into creating schemes that protect an algorithm against
side channel attacks. To date, masking is the most widely discussed construction [CJRR99,
ISW03, PR13, CGLS20], using a linear (XOR-based) random encoding to whiten the
leakage profile of software and hardware. Such a whitening is used as a main mecha-
nism in different cryptographic contexts, from One-Time Pad (OTP) in cryptographic
applications [Sha49] to black-box constructions such as interactive protocols [HLVA02],
and in state-of-the-art SCA-aware NIST-finalist symmetric constructions such as AS-
CON [DEMS21]. Therefore, conducting a thorough analysis of the side-channel character-
istics of a simple XOR operation implementation is highly important.
    Masking/ sharing schemes are not perfectly secure, especially when intermediate values
are known. It is straightforward to extract secret information using high-order attacks
(e.g., [CPRR13])– attacks that cross-correlate leakages from different time-samples with
the intermediate values (masked or not), giving a score to each sub-key before they are
ranked. Even in a more restrictive case where intermediate values are not known, attacks
that compound information from different time-samples, such as Algebraic Side-Channel
Attacks [RSVC09] can extract the key. An Algebraic attack uses (e.g.,) a SAT solver that,
given a Hamming Weight characterization of the leakages and a formulaic characterization
of the algorithm used, the correct key can be solved for. This type of attack has inherent
limitations related to the number of available constraints that are related to the key,
the device’s noise profile, and the ability to correctly map each leakage sample to its
corresponding Hamming Weight.
    Consequently, to date, no adversary was able to extract the secret key from leakages of
only a (very) small number of operations without having access to intermediate values,
particularly when protected schemes are used. Fig. 1 illustrates five reference scenarios
for which leakages are obtained from a simple XOR operation: cryptographic solutions
where sensitive information is XORed with a known intermediate (such as scenarios 1 and
3 in Fig. 1) are known to be vulnerable to attacks such as CPA, template, or MI-attacks
[BCO04, CRR03, GBTP08a]. But as far as we know, there has been no thorough discussion
about the potential adversaries for solutions where sensitive information is XORed with an
unknown intermediate (such as scenarios 3, 4, or 5 in Fig. 1), namely leakage of sharing
with an unknown mask and masked or refreshed XOR.
    In this paper, we introduce a methodology for leveraging side channel traces by
discarding two implicit assumptions commonly made during the leakage modeling stage
of many classic attacks. The first assumption, which we dub the symmetric leakages
assumption, assumes that different instances of the same logic gate produce the same
leakage. Under this assumption, symmetric operations between a key and unknown value
(such as scenario 3 in Fig. 1) reveal at most the value of HW(k); That is, up to log2 (nk + 1)
bits of information may be extracted about nk -bit keys. Without this assumption, the
theoretical bound on the information extracted about the key is removed, allowing us to
learn it in its entirety in practical cases, as shown in Sec. 6.1. The second assumption
we discard is the additive noise assumption, it is typically stated as L = f (k) + N with
N ⊥ k. This assumption neglects to consider interactions that make it possible to extract
higher-order and more structurally complex information from the leakage, as performed in
Sec. 6.4
    Throughout this paper, we allow an additive decomposition into components whose
distributions may depend on processed values (e.g., switched random variables), and regress
on statistical characteristics, or as we refer to them throughout this paper, ‘features’, of
the distribution. Once we discard the underlying assumptions of the classical models, it
becomes not only possible but also feasible to extract the entire key using these leakages
alone.
    The regression-based profiling methodology originates from Schindler’s stochastic
model [SLP05] which resembles FEbA on an abstract level (to some extent). However, it
differs on key aspects of the attack, we extend the stochastic model along three main axes:
first, we target XOR operations where the intermediates used are inaccessible, utilizing bit
leakage variations for the attack, which were not exploited in for that purpose [SLP05].
The proposed approach differs in the features and how we select them - in its simplest
abstraction, we minimize a metric between some leakage model and a tunable feature of

the distribution, which allows for large-scale data handling, rather than minimizing the
mean leakage difference1 . We also use binary optimization to enable attacks on larger key
sizes, which is beyond the scope of [SLP05]. Importantly, we develop concrete bounds and
analytical evaluation of the attack, while also providing rigorous statistical techniques to
reduce complexity with verifiability and explainability. For the degenerated base scenario -
with known intermediates, which is less interesting, and targeting a simple mean leakage
characteristics, FEbA are functionally similar to Schindler’s stochastic model, with the
main differences: the search metric being generated from the attack trace’s covariance, the
loss function, and the provided bounds.
    Compared to previous works, our methodology is resource-efficient, as it reduces attacks
to a scalable optimization problem. For attacks like Template attacks [CRR03], mutual
information attacks [GBTP08a] and neural network the cost is clear: the attack complexity
will grow quickly in regards to one/ many of the following parameters: the number of
attack traces (n), number of key bits (nk ), number of leakage traces (T ), trace leakage
length (l), number of Points of Interest (POIs) in the leakage considered (d), size of
oscilloscope alphabet (|X|) and perhaps more device or attack specific variables. The
attack we propose remains stable for increments in all of the parameters above, with two
caveats: our usage of a heuristic optimization algorithm for key sizes > 32 and difficulty
with handling constrained space searches (models dependent on f (k) for a complicated
f s).
    In this paper, we examine how to abstract leakage in a formal and usable way, enabling
us to reason about it effectively. We leverage it to gain practical insight into the (in)security
of concrete cryptographic schemes and the (in)security of masking and XOR whitening. In
the remainder of this work, we use the term feature to refer to an estimator that captures
the leakage characteristics associated with a specific key and, when applicable, plaintext.



1.1    Our Contribution
The main contribution of this paper is the definition of a new class of side-channel attacks,
termed feature estimation based attacks (FEbAs), along with several demonstrations of
its application. These attacks are built upon a probabilistic approach, which bounds and
significantly reduces the key-guessing space by comparing features of the attack leakages
to a profiled model. Following this rationale, it is possible to construct multiple adversaries
flexibly and analyze their theoretical performance for different targets, potentially target-
ing different protection schemes, different algorithmic assumptions, different adversarial
limitations, and more. Concretely, referring to Fig. 2 FEbAs contribute to the concept of
profiling features as illustrated in Step 3 and Step 4. These two contributions allow us to
create a leakage profile with more fidelity in a low number of traces, even for a vast key
space (Sec. 6.3). This methodology converts side channel attacks to a discrete optimization
problem with continuous parameters, and does so in such a way that theoretical analysis
of the target is possible before knowledge of the attack traces. It also allows us to leverage
traces without access to intermediate values to create an attack (Sec. 6.1). Finally, feature
estimation attacks are built to be computationally feasible even for large key/data-space
attacks that would require too many resources otherwise. A high-level overview of the
experiments performed to highlight the different features of FEbA and their results are
summarized in Table 3. The main theorem of this paper, discussing an apriori theoretical
trace analysis on a nominal target, can be seen in Sec. 1 (Theorem 1) along the result that

3.1     The rational
The rationale is composed of the ideas that resulted in our definitions and methodology
(presented throughout the paper). Namely, (1) the characterization of leakage as a function
of different random variables whose usage depends on the algorithm parameters (2) the
usage of strict probability bounds as a means for key evaluation (3) the reducability of the
key evaluation part to simple models that are optimizable efficiently, (4) usage of features
of the leakage as a means to leverage different independent signal sources on the key.
    These points are furthered elaborated throughout the paper:
   1. The criteria for usable ‘feature estimators’ as listed in Sec. 2.2.
   2. The adversary attack procedure steps in Sec. 4.
   3. Usage of ΣW , ΣL , ΣZ as evaluation metrics (such as done in Appendix A.5). To rate
       the keys by comparing the estimated quantities that bound the posterior probability
       (with some probability).
    In the rest of this section, we elaborate on these ideas and exemplify them when
discussing the simplest feature estimation attack on Ak (;r) = k ⊕ r where k is the secret
key, and r is an unknown randomly generated word.
    The critical and implicit (conventional) assumption we shed is the symmetry of the
leakage. That is, we show that the amount of leakage each bit contributes to the trace
varies. Although it might seem like a minor modification, it actually results in increasing
the limit of the information bits learned from ≤ log2 (nk + 1) (the weight of the word) to
nk , especially when considering how the leakage variations change across different leakage
time samples.
    The second assumption we shed is the additivity of noise (i.e., the assumption that
L = f (k) + N with N ⊥k). We assume our leakage model to be a sum of different random
variables that are switched on or off based on the state of every input and output of every
logic gate in the calculation. For example, k ⊕ r has four possible states (one per possible
input), influencing three leakage variables (two inputs, one output, at least in the way we
characterize it) per key bit, per time sample.

6.0.2      Comparison to algebraic side channel attacks

ASCA [RSVC09] falls under the category of attacks that reduce its leakages to an opti-
mization problem whose solution is hopefully the key, given knowledge of the algorithm
and a simple profiling. Feature estimation-based attacks also fall under this category.
    While FEbA shares conceptual similarities with ASCA in that aspect, ASCA differs in
its requirements, analysis, and more. ASCA attacks on a trace-by-trace basis, because it
requires capturing information from a large number of operations and considers a large set
of constraints, usually targeting a single trace. ASCA also requires a high enough SNR to
bring the expected maximal hamming weight error from a trace to a low enough value,
which would still require the use of an error-tolerant solver.
    FEbA operates on the statistical features of a distribution, which allows it to ‘denoise’
the traces, thereby leveraging them while solving for the key using a discrete minimization
problem instead of a discrete satisfiability problem. The use of leakage features makes the
attack intrinsically error-solvent. This presents a potential improvement beyond ASCA,
where we may leverage every single leakage time-sample for the attack, even multiple
different leakages per operation, instead of those that only leak like the (e.g.,) Hamming
weight of an operation.
    As such, while there are similarities between these attacks, they are not directly
comparable. Comparison to other adversaries may be found in Appendix A.1

7    Summary and Discussion
This paper proposes a new side-channel attack methodology called Feature Estimation
based Attacks (FEbA), which exploits asymmetric leakage in simple XOR operations (for
example, masked key XOR with a random mask). We show that a standalone XOR, and
even a masked implementation (d = 2), can exhibit exploitable, key-dependent leakage in
practical implementations. We show that the magnitude of this information can depend
strongly on micro-architectural realization and operand handling (e.g., operand order), as
observed empirically. We hypothesize that with higher sampling rates, the effectiveness of
this attack increases nonlinearly. Additionally, we note that for low-bandwidth operations
(e.g., 8-bit XORs) our attack will be highly effective. Our conclusions should be interpreted
as a need for caution with the idea that simple or linear operations (especially when
masked) are hard to exploit by side channels, affecting various classical schemes’ design
choices. Alternatively said, it highlights the risk of assuming a leakage function that
holds a symmetric or low-entropy structure (for modeling or attack simplicity) to carry a
significant amount of information.

A.1.1    Model Based Attacks
Model-based attacks are attacks that use a leakage model that compares a set derived
from intermediate values (as a function of a key guess) to a set derived from the attack
leakages by assigning a rank to the notion of how much both sets ‘match’.
    Attacks like CPA [Man04], MCP-DPA [MS16], and MIA [GBTP08b] all fit the criteria.
The concept of these attacks is to compare the intermediate values received by all key
guesses to the leakage and find the optimal key (with or without any initial profiling).
    For these types of attacks, the feature looks as follows:

                        θk ({ℓi , pi }i ) = comp({model(pi , k), f (ℓi )}i )

     where f (ℓ) is some pre-processing of ℓ, model is a function whose statistics is supposed
to ‘align’ with f (ℓ) for the correct key, and comp is a procedure that is supposed to
evaluate the statistic.
     For example, for CPA targeting AES, we get that model(pi , k) = HW(SBOX(pi ⊕ k)),
f (ℓ) = ℓ, comp({vi , ℓi }i ) = maxj |ρ(v, ℓi [j])|. MIA is the same as CPA but with a different
comparison function, and MCP-DPA is the same as CPA, but with a profiled model and f
being a moment calculator. Finally, we pick the key with the largest feature, implicitly
assuming (by our convention) that Pk|X is monotonically increasing with respect to θ.
     The difference between this attack and ours (from the perspective of our rationale, which
is discussed below) is mainly attributed to three factors, which are discussed rigorously
below:
    1. The feature estimation is dependent on the key, making the key-guessing strategy
       computationally difficult for big (sub) keys.
    2. Complicated features, making it difficult to mathematically bound this setup.
    3. Difficult to coherently incorporate multiple ‘features’ at once.
    4. Usually neglects to encode leakage asymmetry (not necessary for known p).

A.1.2    Profile Based Attacks
Profile-based attacks are attacks that characterize a probability distribution and guess
based on it. Examples are template attacks, TA [CRR02], or neural-networks (NN) based
attacks (e.g., [KPH+ 19]).

    From a feature estimation perspective, profiling attacks, explicitly assume a distribution
L̂ given parameters and regress the parameters to fit L⋆ , instead of pattern matching wk⋆
to ŵk . In profiling attacks, leakage equivalence classes are used to lower the profiling (and

    As for key guessing, profile attacks try to estimate the key based on the evaluated
probability, without using bounds as we did. For completeness, we note that profile attacks

the different µ, Σ’s and attack accordingly.
    Once again, this results in disadvantages similar to those attributed to CPA.
   1. The characterization of the model depends on the key and is heuristically assumed

   2. The model depends on the key in a complicated fashion, which may result in an
       inability to leverage the model’s structure to search for keys efficiently for larger key

   • We can arbitrarily add more features to our estimator in a mathematically concise

A.2    Modeling abstraction
During an attack, different useful quantities can be considered, which were defined above:
  1. The expected value of the estimation of the FLD, fk⋆ - the value of the feature which

     every key k.
  2. The estimated feature of the FLD, wk⋆ - the estimated value of fk⋆ using finite profiling
     traces.
  3. The expected value of the estimation of the profiled model, fˆk - the leakage model
     obtained from an asymptotically (number of profiling traces) profiled model.
  4. The estimated feature of the profiled model ŵk - the estimated value of fˆk using
     finite profiling traces.

A.4.2    The Effective Value of l
Looking at ΣZ , it is reasonable to call each eigenvector a feature, with its effectiveness being
the corresponding eigenvalue. Since ΣZ is symmetric (it is also semi-positive definite),
every feature is independent of the other, synonymous with assuming that the list of
eigenvalues of the matrix represents the strengths of independent sources of information
on the key.
    The effective value of l, lef f , is the number of such eigenvectors with eigenvalues that
are not too small. i.e., the number of eigenvalues that result in a non-negligible amount of
information on the key (as a function of the number of traces n, and the accuracy of the
model L̂).
    A single feature may extract the entire key, but the difficulty of extracting B bits of
information from a single features grows as B increases, since averaging over traces reduces
the variance only by a factor of 1/n and there might be billions of keys.
    Due to how ΣW is defined, it will have at most nk − 1 non-zero eigenvalues. This
means that lef f is bound by nk . For the attack to work, we need a good enough model


                                                    33
and/or enough traces for each feature to result in ≈ 1 bits of information about the key in
average.
    Usually, increasing the scope sampling rate by a factor of 2 would imply either ‘a ×2
reduction in the number of traces due to better noise filtering’ or ‘a potential benefit if we
obtained a slightly better POI’. In feature estimation attacks, due to the inherent instability
of leakages near the leakage’s peak (which also depends on the adjacent operations), such
an improvement would also introduce a new orthogonal feature, which would augment
one of the signal of one of the eigenvector with a small eigenvalue in ΣZ (with some
probability). This has the potential to improve the complexity of the attack in the number
of traces needed - beyond what a ×2 noise reduction would give us.
